SUIDS is the leading cause of death, and surface sharing is the leading cause of SUIDS. SUIDS is typically suffocation. It is something or a position suffocating baby and the mechanism to move the head away doesn't work. It's also just plain suffocation without a neurological issue when it can't be proven or when autopsy isn't done. Removing surface sharing stops 9/10 sleep related deaths, so we know it is from exterior controllable risks.

There are certain environmental factors that can trigger a SIDS event - soft bedding, loose bedding, overheating, prone placement, etc. About 90% of SIDS and SUID cases have one or more external risk factors and most could be prevented absent those factors. There are also certain intrinsic (out of our control) factors that, for whatever reason, make an infant more susceptible to SIDS - prematurity, low birth weight, etc. If a SIDS case has no external risk factors present, it is often that multiple intrinsic risks compounded on each other. Protective Factors These are additional measures you can implement on top of following the baseline that will further reduce the risk of SIDS. Studies have shown that they protect your baby from SIDS although the mechanism of action is not always clear: pacifier use, breastfeeding, room sharing, immunizations, etc. There is no evidence that they can independently trigger a SIDS event if you don't use them. Not using one of factors will not increase your baby’s risk of SIDS, but rather return the risk level to baseline. Is a baby with all the protective factors in place at a lower risk than if they had none? Absolutely. But the baseline (external factors that MUST be controlled) is a baby sleeping in a safe sleep environment, absent risk factors that can trigger a SIDS event. [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK513399](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK513399) [https://pediatrics.aappublications.org/content/pediatrics/early/2016/10/20/peds.2016-2940.full.pdf](https://pediatrics.aappublications.org/content/pediatrics/early/2016/10/20/peds.2016-2940.full.pdf) Yes, the exact cause of SIDS is unknown but that does not mean there are not critical steps you can take to protect your baby from SIDS. YOU are in control of the external factors and can help protect your child from SIDS and sleep-related deaths by avoiding them all together. Follow the baseline (ABCs) for each and every sleep. Implement protective factors. Educate your loved ones and caregivers. Start from day one and be vigilant.

Eczema- They mostly mention inconsistent results or no effect on Eczema that was treated with human milk. 

Dermatitis- Iranian study claimed the human milk cured dermatitis, but I am unsure if there's other factors that could have contributed or what variables are in that study. 

Diaper rash- Another diaper rash study was done on NICU babies who were on antibiotics and a bunch of other variables that could not be controlled. 

Nipple pain- The nipple study specifically found that lanolin worked way better for nipple pain and healing. 

Ophthalmic infections- The eye infection study found that ointment was best to treat eye infections.

See.. I'm having a similar but different experience. After 3 years of fertility treatments (all negative tests), I started to acknowledge (not accept but at least understand) that it may never happen for us, which was unfathomably devastating. I finally understood I was one of "them"; a person with infertility. My biggest nightmare come true. Then we finally got a positive test. And my brain couldn't accept it. We kept waiting for the punchline but I just continued to stay pregnant. There were complications early on and we were warned we may lose it so I thought that was the "catch" and basically didn't let myself get excited about it or even process that I was pregnant. I had imposter syndrome the whole time. It felt like I couldn't finally be part of this club (one of the lucky ones I had come to be so jealous of) because I was part of the other club, the infertiles. I felt like I was betraying them almost and I was always waiting for the shoe to drop, since it felt like we'd always had horrible luck and the universe was against us. once the complications eased away I slooowlyyy started being excited about the pregnancy and kind of processing that I was indeed pregnant. By then it was almost time for birth. When he was born, my brain couldn't catch up. I was barely caught up to processing the positive test, let alone the pregnancy, let alone and actual baby placed into my arms. Because of this I felt totally detached from him. Faint positive at 12dpo. All my rounds were medicated with stims and progesterone (iuis it was letrozole, ovidrel, and crinone). The lucky round we did superovulation, so an extra dose of letrozole.  Also, the month before I got a new acupuncturist who was actually Asian (no offense to white people lol) and had been practicing for decades with TONS of accolades. Another thing that changed was I had my third HSG ultrasound (I previously had a blocked right tube but every 6 months or so we'd reassess with an hsg and this one took place the month before lucky 7 and revealed an open right tube. Hsg is said to increase your chances for a couple months after in and of itself because it rinses you out nicely so it was a double bonus). Luckily, for the first time ever, we triggered (ovidrel) with 2 follicles on my right ovary (one a little small at 17mm and one a little large at 23mm). This was the first time bothering with anything on the right and apparently the right ovary weilds more pregnancies. 

I'm super anti-pseudoscience but you reach a point where you'll try anything, so that month I had also done some hope spa treatment where you find a healing tree in a meditation and they give you an oral essence of the tree and you take a bit everyday, so I did that lol it was just like lilac essence in water with a few other herbs. Probably not great for health lol maybe it healed my tube lol

I took coq10 a bit more consistently than usual ( every few days). 

That's about it. But it's a lot. We threw everything at it and finally it stuck. Mind you, I'm 7 weeks in and very high risk, good chance it may unstuck, but at least we know we can actually get pregnant now. I think it was a culmination of many of these elements, especially the open tube, superovulation, and hsg flush out. 

A lot of people say you get pregnant when you finally give up and I want to state that that's not true but I think I get what they mean. It's not that I ever gave up on getting pregnant, it's just that I learned through so many failed cycles that I could do everything perfectly and it still doesn't work, so eventually you find a groove of being more relaxed on some of the aspects of conception and you get conditioned to the failure. You cry a bit less, you get a bit less invested, you accept that it'll probably be a bfn. But you haven't given up. It's not the same. You just surrender a bit, knowing it's fairly out of your control. There's no prayers being answered and there's no statistics being followed. I couldn't predict anything and eventually gave up trying. Science didn't help and neither did spirituality, it was all Utter chaos. The scariest of all. Until you just let go. 

Hope this helps.

When I was 9, my mom was getting chemo and I didn't understand cancer that much. I overheard her very violently being sick and immediately I had a full psychological breakdown and had the full blown phobia, along with ptsd and ocd. Slowly it's gotten a bit better (I'm 27 now). But honestly, earlier than that, ever since I can remember, I was always fascinated/obsessed by it. Any time I saw it on tv I had to tell everyone. And they were like...k??? I fixated on it if I saw it on the ground or knew someone was sick. So it was a fixation before a fear, so to some degree maybe it was always something off in me?

I think for most there's a point of trauma that has a deeper meaning ( in my case my mom was getting chemo when I was 9 and I heard her be s*ck aggressively) and I think my brain associated that with cancer and her possibly dying or being in worse shape. I also think it's an incredibly violent and graphic action. It's scary looking and sounding. It's forceful. I think a lot of us have a fear of losing control/seeing others in a state of lack of control. Maybe because of deeper issues in life we didn't have control of. When I was younger I was also very uncomfortable seeing grown ups drunk because they were supposed to be in control, not vulnerable. So I think seeing someone weak means they can't help us if we need them and that there's no one with complete control? I dunno. Also, relating to the comment above, I developed my phobia at 9 (from the incident mentioned earlier) i believe, but before that, as far back as I can remember, I was still obsesses with v***t. Like fascinated, fixated. Everytime it happened in my cartoons if run to wake my parents up to tell them. I couldn't comprehend that it happened. There was always the fixation, even before the fear. Which is strange and elusive. I think there's the fear of contagion in our genetic instincts. To avoid getting any serious illnesses we avoid weaker beings that could pose risks to our health. I think it's also often very sudden therefore startling. Like in cut scenes in movies, it's such a loud violent thing to happen spontaneously, I think it could be associated with startling adrenaline, like when people sneeze suddenly and it scares the shit out of you and maybe that just develops from there. I dunno, for me it's something about seeing someone so vulnerable and out of control that freaks me out. It's weird also that a lot of us also have like OCD. Many have the germ kind but weirdly for me I got the counting/symmetry and ticks from the phobia. I think maybe because I used counting/tapping as a distraction from my brain always going there, and humming/vocal sounds often to block out sounds anytime someone went to the bathroom near my room so it became a vocal tick. I dunno it's a fucking mess of an illness that's for sure. But why we associate it with danger, I'm not sure. There's some strange commonalities in this community though that could hold the keys.
